newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: France wants troops in Zaire for up to two months.
newsitem.headline: France wants troops in Zaire for up to two months.

text.p: France has proposed that the U.N. Security Council approve an intervention force for two months to aid more than a million refugees in eastern Zaire despite hesitations from the European Union and the United States.

Paris' resolution, which is not expected to be adopted this week but was unveiled on Thursday, says that member states "on an urgent and temporary basis" should make necessary arrangements to allow humanitarian aid to refugees, including "protected zones covering limited areas."
It says the costs would be borne by participating member states and that any mission would cooperate with both U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and the Organisation of African Unity.

The troops, to ensure security for aid distribution, would be authorised under Chapter 7 of the U.N. Charter, which allows the use of force, according to the draft document distributed by French envoys to council members.

But diplomats said there would be no vote until key European states as well as the United States came to a decision both on the concept of the force and the states taking part in it. The council, they said, would reflect contacts between world leaders rather than take the initiative.

At the moment only France and Spain have volunteered to send soldiers as part of a proposed 5,000-strong multinational force. The United States, which still has questions on the force, will not contribute any troops but might give logistical aid in transporting soldiers from other nations to the region.

The European Union failed on Thursday to agree on a joint initiative to help the refugees in eastern Zaire. Germany joined other countries in effectively rejecting the Franco-Spanish proposal. Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the task of protecting refugees should be left to African nations. Britain also has not made a final decision but is not expected to send any troops either.

"The council is still not there yet," said Germany's ambassador Tono Eitel. "Whether the French ideas would command the right support that they would need for now remains a bit doubtful but I would wish them success."
"Only the feasibility (of the action) is not yet clear to me," he added.

One problem, according to Eitel, is what kind of supervision would be needed if the refugee camps in eastern Zaire were reconstituted. The camps have been bases for Hutu fighters wanting to overthrow Rwanda's Tutsi-led government.

Hutu army officers and militiamen took a leading role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda in which more than 500,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed. After the Tutsis took over the country, more than a million Hutus fled to Zaire.
In the last two months fighting has broken out with Tutsis who have lived in Zaire for 200 years and local Zaireans, causing the refugees to flee without food and shelter.

Fearing widespread death from starvation and disease, the Security Council for the past two weeks has deliberated on the issue, but its actions were limited to statements calling for a ceasefire to allow aid to get through and international conferences aimed toward a long-term political solution in Central Africa.

France, which set up a safe area in Rwanda briefly in 1994, was sharply criticised by Rwanda's new Tutsi government for sheltering Hutus guilty of genocide. This time Paris wants to make sure other countries participate in equal numbers.
